soil-phys-063.title: Porosity: how much of a soil is empty space
soil-phys-063.text: Solid granite is almost all rock, with less than 0.005 of its volume left empty. Peat and clay can be more than half empty space. That share is porosity: the fraction of a material's total volume taken up by voids, given from 0 to 1 or as a percentage. Geologists, hydrologists and soil scientists use it for any porous medium, such as rock or sediment, whose voids may hold air or water. It is written ϕ or n. Porosity can be worked out from two densities. When the voids hold air, it equals one minus a ratio of two densities. On top is the density of the whole soil, in {{ref:soil-phys-060}}; below is that of its solid grains alone, in {{ref:soil-phys-062}}. Sorting matters as much as grain size. A well-sorted material is more porous than a poorly sorted one of similar size, because in the mixed one small particles fill the gaps between larger ones. A few fine grains lodged in the pores can sharply cut porosity, and the ease of water flow, while making up only a small share of the volume. In rock and sedimentary layers, porosity governs how much water or hydrocarbon they may hold. It also falls with depth. As buried sediment compacts, its porosity drops exponentially, a pattern described by the Athy (1930) equation.

soil-phys-059.title: Soil physics: the science of grains, water and air
soil-phys-059.text: How fast water sinks into a field, how air reaches a root, how warm the ground gets: these are questions for soil physics. It studies the physical properties and processes of soil across its solid, liquid and gas phases. The field borrows from physics, physical chemistry, engineering and meteorology, and turns them on practical problems in agriculture, ecology and engineering. Its results guide management and prediction in natural and managed ecosystems alike. F. H. King ({{ref:soil-hist-020}}), called the father of soil physics in the United States, studied how soils hold water, take in air and move water. Edgar Buckingham (1867–1940) worked out the theory of how gases diffuse through soil and how water flows in the unsaturated ground above the groundwater. Willard Gardner first measured capillary potential with porous cups and manometers. L. A. Richards ({{ref:soil-hist-023}}) described flow in unsaturated soil and measured how tightly soil holds its water with the instrument described in {{ref:soil-water-221}}. Later, John R. Philip found an analytical solution for soil water transport, and Martinus van Genuchten built functions for how soil holds and conducts water.

soil-phys-092.title: Soil mechanics: how a mix of grains, water and air behaves
soil-phys-092.text: A dam, a pipeline and a house foundation all rest on the same question: how will the soil behave? Soil mechanics is the branch of soil physics and applied mechanics that answers it. Unlike fluid or solid mechanics, it deals with a mixture: fluids, usually air and water, among particles of clay, silt, sand and gravel, plus organic solids. With rock mechanics it underpins geotechnical engineering and engineering geology. It analyses how structures built on, made of or buried in soil deform, and how fluids flow inside them, from foundations and retaining walls to dams and pipelines. Agricultural, coastal and geophysical engineering and hydrology use its principles too. One idea runs through it. A load pressing down on soil is shared between the pore fluid and the particles. Neither gas nor liquid resists shear, though, so resistance to sliding comes from friction and interlocking of the grains. Standard classification tests miss part of the story. They use dried, sieved and remoulded samples, so the soil's structure and its pattern of pore sizes and fluids are lost.

soil-phys-060.title: Bulk density: weighing soil with its holes included
soil-phys-060.text: Quartz has a density of about 2.65 g/cm3, yet the dry bulk density of a mineral soil is normally about half that, between 1.0 and 1.6 g/cm3. Bulk density is the mass of a soil divided by the whole volume it occupies, counting the spaces between and within its particles. That last clause separates it from {{ref:soil-phys-062}}, which leaves the voids out. Because it counts the gaps, bulk density depends on packing and changes with handling: a disturbed powder settles to a higher value. In soil it depends mainly on the mineral make-up and on how compacted the soil is. Organic soils sit at the light end. Soils rich in organic carbon and some crumbly clays fall below 1.0 g/cm3, and peat soils range from 0.02 to 0.98 g/cm3. Dark, well-decomposed organic matter lowers it too. The rule is simple: the more pore space a soil has, the lower its dry bulk density. A high value points either to compaction or to a mix of textures in which small particles fill the voids between coarse ones. Measured at a standard moisture content, bulk density estimates compaction. A European Union study of the top 0-20 cm found croplands almost 1.5 times denser than woodlands. Simple formulas also combine bulk density with particle size to estimate properties such as how readily water flows through soil.

soil-phys-120.title: The soil matrix, the solid frame around the pores
soil-phys-120.text: The soil matrix is the solid phase of a soil: the mineral particles and organic matter that make it up. Around it lie the pore space, holding the soil atmosphere, and the soil solution, holding water and dissolved substances. Matrix particles are classed by size and by mineral make-up. Texture largely sets how water moves and is held, but mineralogy can strongly modify both. Gravel, sand and silt usually inherit their minerals from the parent material, most often weathering-resistant quartz. Clay is the most active part, with a high specific surface area and unbalanced negative charges, so its mineralogy matters most. Its minerals are secondary, precipitates that keep forming as long as the soil exists. The organic part of the matrix, weight for weight, holds many times more exchangeable positive ions than clay. Nutrients held this way, such as K, Ca, Mg, P and Zn, form a ready reservoir for plants.

soil-phys-069.title: Pore space, where soil keeps its water and air
soil-phys-069.text: Roots, burrowing animals and microbes all live in the gaps. Pore space is the part of a soil's volume not filled by solid mineral and organic particles, and it holds the soil's water and air. Total porosity is the pore volume divided by the total volume, often given in percent; in unsaturated soil, air and water share it. A sandy soil is more porous than a silty sand, because silt fills the gaps between sand grains. When water soaks in, the largest cracks and pores fill first, mostly by gravity. Smaller pores fill slowly by capillary forces and can trap air. Large pores and cracks largely control how fast water enters and moves. They also strongly affect gas exchange and the breathing of soil life. The ease of water movement through pores, {{ref:soil-water-193}}, depends on compaction and on how full the pores are. Roots and burrowing animals carve networks of connected pores. Microbial cells and their slime can also block pores, a process described in {{ref:soil-water-241}}.

soil-phys-082.title: Soil compaction: squeezing the air out of the ground
soil-phys-082.text: In one cotton field, the tilled surface soil had a bulk density of 1.3 g/cm3 and 51% pore space. Between the rows, where wheels ran, it reached 1.67 g/cm3, and pore space fell to 37%. That is soil compaction: the densification of soil under applied stress as air is pushed out of the pores between its grains. When water rather than air is squeezed out, the process is consolidation, described in {{ref:soil-phys-110}}. In soil science and agronomy the word compaction usually covers both, and suction as water evaporates can drive it too. Heavy machinery is the usual cause, though the passage of animal feet can also compact soil. The damage follows from the lost pores. Pressed-together grains leave little room for the air and water roots need, and burrowing animals struggle to penetrate the denser soil. Compacted soil absorbs less rainfall, so runoff and erosion increase and less water recharges the groundwater. Recovery depends on climate, mineralogy and the animals living in the soil. Soils that shrink and swell strongly, such as those in {{ref:soil-class-106}}, recover quickly where dry spells shrink and crack them. Clays built of a mineral that does not crack as it dries, described in {{ref:soil-chem-088}}, cannot recover unaided. They need earthworms or other ground-dwelling animals living in them, as in the Cecil soils.

soil-phys-086.title: The hidden damage under farm fields
soil-phys-086.text: Erosion is easy to see. Compaction mostly is not. Unlike salt build-up or erosion, compaction of farmland is mainly a hidden problem below the surface, and finding it takes special methods. Soil compaction in agriculture is the rise in bulk density, or fall in porosity, of farmland soil under loads from outside or within. It is also called soil structure degradation. It can harm nearly all the physical, chemical and biological properties and functions of soil. Together with erosion it has been called the costliest and most serious environmental problem of conventional agriculture. Heavy machinery and poor management can press the subsoil into impermeable layers that hold back the movement of water and nutrients. On the farm, compaction cuts crop growth, yield and quality. Beyond it, compaction adds runoff, erosion, greenhouse gas emissions, nutrients fouling lakes and rivers, less water reaching the groundwater, and loss of biodiversity. The problem is old. Hard layers below the plough, described in {{ref:soil-agri-101}}, were linked to compaction before farming was mechanized, and modern techniques have raised the risk. In 1991 compaction was estimated at 4% of human-caused damage to soils worldwide, some 68.3 million hectares. In 2013 it was a major cause of damage in Europe (about 33 million ha), Africa (18 million ha), Asia (10 million ha) and Australia (4 million ha). In Europe about 32% of subsoils are highly vulnerable to it and 18% moderately so.

soil-phys-098.title: Pore water pressure, the push of water between grains
soil-phys-098.text: Water held between soil grains pushes back. Pore water pressure is the pressure of the groundwater in the pores between the particles of a soil or rock. Deep in saturated ground it is measured with piezometers. Where the water is not flowing it is close to hydrostatic, rising steadily with depth. The surface where it equals atmospheric pressure is the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. Above that level, capillarity sets the pressure, and it is called tension, suction or matric pressure. Instruments with a porous ceramic cup in contact with the soil measure it there, by methods set out in ISO 11276:1995. The pressure has several parts: the weight of overlying material, osmotic pressure from uneven ion concentrations, and adsorption pressure from water films that draw particles together. It matters because the load carried by the grains, {{ref:soil-phys-100}}, is the total stress minus the pore water pressure. Too much of it can force blocks out at the base of river banks, and rising pressure on slopes helps burst the surface layer, as in {{ref:soil-phys-160}}.

soil-phys-073.title: Void ratio: comparing the gaps with the grains
soil-phys-073.text: Porosity divides empty space by the whole volume. Void ratio divides it by the solids alone. It is the ratio of the volume of voids, filled with gas or liquid, to the volume of solids, a dimensionless number closely tied to porosity. Geotechnical engineers treat it, as the symbol e, as a state variable of soils. Because they use ϕ for the angle of shearing resistance, they write porosity as η. Void ratio predicts behaviour under load. A loose soil with a high void ratio tends to shrink as voids close and grain contacts multiply. A dense soil with a low void ratio tends to swell when unloaded. Loose soils conduct water readily, and dense ones less so. Fine particles pass through the large voids of loose soil but clog the small pores of dense soil. For a given soil, the ease with which water passes rises with the void ratio. The simple relation assumes a rigid skeleton that keeps its volume on wetting and drying. Swelling clays such as {{ref:soil-chem-091}}, with water bound between their layers, fall outside it.

soil-phys-100.title: Effective stress: the load the grains really carry
soil-phys-100.text: Soil grains do not carry the whole weight above them. Effective stress is the part of the total stress in a soil carried by its solid skeleton rather than by the pore water. Karl von Terzaghi first proposed, in 1925, that it equals the total normal stress minus the pore water pressure. It governs both the strength and the volume change of porous media, from sand to concrete. Soil strength comes mainly from friction between particles, which is proportional to the stress pressing them together. So when pore water pressure rises, strength falls. Pore water is nearly incompressible, so saturated soil can pack closer only if water is squeezed out. Water injected between grains pushes them apart and lowers effective stress; withdrawing it forces them together. {{ref:soil-phys-118}} and the sandcastle effect mark the two extremes. Effective stress is central to the stability of slopes and to land sinking from groundwater pumping. Yet in 1962 Jennings and Burland showed that partly saturated soils do not follow effective stress alone.

soil-phys-125.title: Seepage: water on the move through soil
soil-phys-125.text: Still water in soil does little harm. Moving water can bring down a levee. Seepage is the movement of water through soil. Below the {{ref:soil-water-247}}, where pore water pressure rises evenly with depth, conditions are hydrostatic and nothing flows. A sloping or perched water surface sets water seeping. The rate follows {{ref:soil-water-201}}. Flow is proportional to how fast excess pressure changes with distance, scaled by how freely the soil passes water and by the fluid's viscosity. The ease of flow varies enormously, from about 10−12 m/s in clays to about 10−1 m/s in gravels. In steady seepage, velocities do not change with time; that does not hold while water levels are changing or the soil is consolidating. Upward seepage lowers effective stress. At the critical hydraulic gradient it reaches zero, the soil loses nearly all strength, and less permeable layers may heave. This state, also called a boiling condition, is the one behind {{ref:soil-phys-116}} and {{ref:soil-phys-118}}. Strength lost to upward seepage often helps cause levee failures. Fast seepage also drags particles away from where it comes out. The erosion works back upslope as soil piping, which can fail a structure and open sinkholes. To stop seepage below dams, engineers build impermeable curtains of {{ref:soil-chem-100}}, a clay almost fully saturated with sodium.

soil-phys-101.title: Shear strength: how hard soil can be pushed before it fails
soil-phys-101.text: Whether a slope stands or a bridge settles too far comes down to one property. Shear strength is the largest shear stress a soil can sustain before it fails. Resistance comes from friction and interlocking of particles, and sometimes from cement or bonds where they touch. Friction dominates, so resistance on a plane is roughly proportional to the effective normal stress. That makes the angle of internal friction close to the steepest slope at which loose grains will pile. Strength also depends on drainage, how densely particles pack, and the rate and direction of strain. Interlocked grains make soil expand or contract as it shears. If it expands, density and strength drop, so a peak may be followed by falling shear stress. Eventually shear stress and density hold constant while strain continues, a condition called the critical state, steady state or residual strength. If water cannot flow in or out, shearing is undrained: density cannot change, but pore pressure and effective stress do. Real soils are partly drained.

soil-phys-116.title: Liquefaction: when shaking turns solid ground to liquid
soil-phys-116.text: In the 2018 Palu earthquake, the ground itself flowed. It buried the suburb of Balaroa and Petobo village 3 metres deep in mud. Soil liquefaction is the sudden loss of strength and stiffness in a wet soil of loose, unbound grains. Under stress such as earthquake shaking, the solid behaves like a liquid. Loose sand tends to compress under load. If it is saturated, pore water pressure rises until it exceeds the contact forces between grains, and effective stress falls to essentially zero. Dense sands dilate instead. So the soils most at risk are loose, saturated, poorly drained sands and non-plastic silts; gravels and clays rarely liquefy. Young Holocene beds of well-sorted sand and silt, saturated and metres thick, along stream beds, beaches, dunes and loess areas, are the most susceptible. Allen Hazen first called soil 'liquefied' after the 1918 failure of the Calaveras Dam in California. Engineers paid closer attention after the 1964 Alaska and Niigata earthquakes. Shaking can force water and liquefied sand to the surface, and ground can slide sideways on slopes of only 1 or 2 degrees, called lateral spreading. Liquefaction damages buildings, bridges, buried services and levees. Over geological time it may also leave a dense parent material in which a fragipan can develop. Engineers fight it by densifying soil with vibro or dynamic compaction or stabilising it with grout, and cementing sand with calcite made by microbes has been proposed.

soil-phys-118.title: Quicksand, solid until it is disturbed
soil-phys-118.text: At about 2 grams per cubic centimetre, quicksand is roughly twice as dense as the human body, so a person cannot sink beyond about waist height. It is a colloid of fine sand, silt or clay and water that forms when saturated loose sand is agitated and loses its strength. Upward flow, as from an artesian spring, holds the grains suspended. Undisturbed it looks solid, but a change in stress of less than 1% suddenly makes it runny. Pulling a foot out at 1 cm/s takes as much force as lifting a car. Slow movements and floating on the back allow escape.

soil-phys-107.title: Cohesion: the strength that is not friction
soil-phys-107.text: Friction explains most of a soil's strength, but not all of it. Cohesion is the part of a soil's or rock's shear strength that does not depend on friction between particles. In soils it comes from electrostatic forces in stiff clays that once bore heavier loads, from cementing by Fe2O3, CaCO3 or NaCl, and from negative capillary pressure. The pore pressure response when water cannot drain adds some, and so do plant roots. Several sources are temporary. Weathering can remove electrostatic bonds, wetting removes capillary suction, time dissipates pore pressure, and logging or fire removes root strength. Mohr–Coulomb theory usually measures cohesion as the shear strength at zero normal pressure on the failure surface. Values run from 0 to 48 kPa for very soft clay, through 192 to 384 kPa for stiff clay, to 384 to 766 kPa for very stiff clay. When soil loses cohesion it can slough off banks and slopes.

soil-phys-110.title: Consolidation: the slow squeeze that sinks buildings
soil-phys-110.text: Picture a spring inside a water-filled container with a hole in its lid. Press the lid and at first the water resists. Then it drains out through the hole, and the spring shortens and takes over the load. The spring is the soil skeleton. The process is soil consolidation. It is the gradual change in a soil's volume under a change in pressure, as water is slowly squeezed out of or drawn into its pores. When saturated soil is loaded, the water, far stiffer in volume than the skeleton, first carries the load as excess pore water pressure. As it seeps away, the grains take the load and the soil shrinks. Saturated clays consolidate very slowly, because water passes through them with extreme difficulty. Coarse soils drain readily and settle at once instead. Clays settle under external loads, under their own weight or that of overlying soil, and when groundwater pumping raises the effective stress on them. The effects show most where a building sits on soft, poorly permeable soil such as marine clay, which can settle a great deal over many years. In the narrow sense the term means this delayed, drainage-driven response. In the broad sense it covers any pressure-driven volume change, including compaction, sinking land, heave and swelling. Karl von Terzaghi, the 'father of soil mechanics', defined it as any loss of water from a saturated soil without air taking its place. Engineers measure it with the oedometer test, loading a thin disc of soil in steps and recording its thickness over time.

soil-phys-109.title: Angle of repose: the steepest slope a pile can hold
soil-phys-109.text: Wind-blown sand piles up to about 34 degrees before it slides. That limit is the angle of repose, the steepest angle from the horizontal at which a granular material can be piled without slumping. Rough grains pile more steeply than rounded ones. A little water bridging the gaps raises the angle, but saturation lubricates the grains and can set slopes moving. Typical values are 15° for wet excavated clay, 15–30° for water-filled sand and 25–30° for natural gravel with sand. Henri Gautier recognized this 'natural slope' of soils in 1717.

soil-phys-095.title: How water climbs above the groundwater
soil-phys-095.text: Water in soil does not stop at the {{ref:soil-water-247}}. It climbs into the small pores above, held there by surface tension under negative pressure. This is capillary action in soil. For some distance above that level the soil can be fully saturated; higher up it is still wet, but holds less water with every step of height. Pore size sets the climb, from about a centimetre in coarse sand to tens of metres in silt or clay. Water held at negative pressure pulls particles together, so effective stress can stay positive even at a free surface. That is why a wet sand castle stands, held by friction where grains touch, and collapses once it is submerged. Negative pore pressures are much stronger in clay than in sand. They explain why clay soils shrink as they dry and swell when wetted, which can damage light structures and roads.

soil-phys-115.title: Overburden pressure, the weight of everything above
soil-phys-115.text: Overburden pressure is the pressure at a given depth caused by the weight of the overlying material, also called lithostatic pressure or vertical stress. It increases with depth in proportion to the density of the overlying material and gravity; in the Earth's crust the average gradient is about 270 bar/km. It squeezes pores smaller, shrinking volume without distorting the material, so it matters as sediment hardens into rock and as rock is transformed. Hard-to-measure sideways stresses are expressed relative to it through a coefficient, k. Together with excess pore water pressure, overburden can force blocks out near the base of a river bank, a popout failure.

openers.density-pores-and-compaction: A handful of soil is partly nothing at all: empty spaces that hold its water and air. This chapter measures that emptiness and asks what happens when weight squeezes it out. Soil physics studies the solid, liquid and gas phases of soil, and soil mechanics describes how a mix of particles, water and air behaves under load. Porosity, bulk density and the ratio of voids to solids track how tightly the solid particles pack. When machines or loads press them closer, air and water are driven out, and the balance between the push of water in the pores and the stress on the grains decides whether the ground stands firm or flows.
